effect_estimate.comment: Robustness checks using normalized percentile ranks (Table 4), aggregate institutional indices Inst(1) = 0.206 (p = 0.067) and Inst(3) = 0.715 (p = 0.074) (Table 5), time fixed effects (Table 6), and endogenous-institution specifications (Table 7, all six indicators positive with p <= 0.029) confirm positive associations. In rural–urban gap models (Table 9), Voice and Accountability widens the urban–rural gap (0.657, p = 0.006 domestic; 0.832, p = 0.014 foreign) whereas Government Effectiveness (-1.062, p = 0.000), Regulatory Quality (-1.171, p = 0.002), Rule of Law (-1.351, p = 0.005), and Political Stability (-0.557, p = 0.006) narrow it.
effect_estimate.value: In baseline two-step system GMM regressions with domestic controls (N = 44 countries, 541 observations), a 1-unit (standard normal) increase in Voice and Accountability, Regulatory Quality, or Control of Corruption increases the percentage of the population with access to improved sanitation by 0.141 percentage points (p = 0.016), 0.173 percentage points (p = 0.010; 10.8 percentage points in the long run), and 0.295 percentage points (p = 0.058; 10.2 percentage points in the long run) in the short run, respectively, whereas Political Stability (0.106, p = 0.296), Government Effectiveness (0.292, p = 0.109), and Rule of Law (0.174, p = 0.151) are not statistically significant. Adding foreign controls (aid and FDI, 513 observations), Voice and Accountability (0.228, p = 0.022) and Control of Corruption (0.259, p = 0.018) remain statistically significant. Disaggregating rural and urban areas (domestic controls) reveals a dichotomy: in rural areas, Control of Corruption (0.402, p = 0.001), Rule of Law (0.232, p = 0.026), Regulatory Quality (0.184, p = 0.020), and Government Effectiveness (0.258, p = 0.075) significantly increase sanitation access while Voice and Accountability (0.119, p = 0.169) does not; in urban areas, only Voice and Accountability has a statistically significant positive effect (0.283, p = 0.015; 0.254, p = 0.011 with foreign controls).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 9–11, Section IV, Tables 2–3; PDF pp. 14–16, Section V, Tables 8–9

mechanism_certainty.comment: Documented statistical association (level 1) between aggregate country-level World Governance Indicator perception scores and national/rural/urban sanitation access rates. Specific administrative or legal mechanisms are not directly observed empirically, and the authors explicitly note that WGI measures perceptions rather than specific formal institutional designs (PDF p. 13) and that the study relies on aggregated data and does not establish causality (PDF p. 17).

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines six macro-level World Governance Indicators: Voice and Accountability (citizens' participation in selecting government and freedom of expression/association to advocate for basic needs: participation), Rule of Law and Control of Corruption (contract enforcement, courts, police, and curbing exercise of public power for private gain: ENFORCEMENT), and Government Effectiveness and Regulatory Quality (civil service policy formulation/implementation, regulatory quality, and coordination among governmental institutions and local communities: DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, political_coordination).

evidence_quotes.quote: We employ dynamic panel estimation to uncover the empirical relationship between institutions and access to sanitation in sub-Sahara Africa. We find that control of corruption, regulatory quality, and voice and accountability increase access to sanitation.
We employ panel data of 44 SSA countries from 2002 to 2015 for our empirical analysis.
Access to improved sanitation is measured by the percentage of the population with access and using improved sanitation facilities.

Moreover, a dichotomy exists between rural and urban areas in that efficient corruption control, rule of law, and government effectiveness facilitate access to sanitation in rural areas. However, only voice and accountability matter in urban areas.
However, the study depends on aggregated data and does not establish causality between institutions and sanitation.
